title: Phalanges of the hand
source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb (and glossary); 8.5; 9.4; 9.5; 20.5

main.t: The 14 bones of the fingers and thumb (phalanges).

simpler.t: The phalanges are the bones of your fingers and thumb.

deeper.t: The name comes from the Greek “phalanx”, a rectangular block of soldiers.

facts.t: The thumb (digit 1) has two: a proximal and a distal phalanx.
Each finger, digits 2 to 5, has three: proximal, middle and distal.
The proximal phalanges meet the heads of the metacarpals at the knuckles.

simpler.t: There are two in your thumb and three in each finger.

deeper.t: The anatomical name for the thumb is the pollex.

items.name: Proximal phalanges
items.t: The nearest to the palm; each meets a metacarpal head at a knuckle joint.

items.name: Middle phalanges
items.t: Only in the fingers, between the proximal and distal phalanges.

items.name: Distal phalanges
items.t: The tips of the fingers and thumb.

items.name: Base, shaft and head
items.t: Each phalanx has a base nearest the palm, a shaft and a head.

simpler.t: Each finger has a near, a middle and an end bone; the thumb has no middle one.

deeper.t: So the thumb has one interphalangeal joint, and each finger has two.

facts.t: Interphalangeal joints are hinge joints: they only bend and straighten.
Knuckle (metacarpophalangeal) joints are condyloid, so the fingers can bend and also spread apart.
Spreading the fingers apart is abduction; bringing them together is adduction.

simpler.t: Knuckle joints bend and spread; the joints along the fingers only bend.

items.name: Metacarpophalangeal (knuckle) joints
items.t: Condyloid joints between the metacarpal heads and the proximal phalanges.

items.name: Metacarpals
items.t: Meet the proximal phalanges at the knuckles.

items.name: Digital arteries
items.t: Branch from the palmar arches to supply the fingers.

items.name: Digital veins
items.t: Drain the fingers into the palmar venous arches.

simpler.t: They hinge on each other and join the palm bones at the knuckles.

facts.t: They form by replacing a cartilage model with bone (endochondral ossification).
Small bones like these develop only one secondary ossification centre, so each has one growth plate.
A growth plate is cartilage, less dense than bone, so it looks dark on an X-ray.

items.injury: A child’s injured finger has an X-ray.
items.damaged: Possibly nothing: each phalanx has a normal growth plate.
items.cannotDo: Rely on one dark line alone to diagnose a fracture.
items.why: Cartilage is less dense than bone, so a normal plate looks dark and can be mistaken for a break.

items.injury: A ball strikes the tip of a straight finger.
items.damaged: The tendon that straightens the fingertip tears from the distal phalanx, sometimes with a fragment of bone (mallet finger).
items.cannotDo: Straighten the tip of the finger.
items.why: Without its tendon, nothing pulls the distal phalanx straight.

items.q: Explain why the thumb has one interphalangeal joint, but each finger has two.
model: The thumb has two phalanges: proximal and distal.
Each finger has three: proximal, middle and distal.
An interphalangeal joint lies between each pair of neighbouring phalanges.
So the thumb has one, and each finger has two.

items.q: Compare the knuckle (metacarpophalangeal) joints with the interphalangeal joints.
model: They allow bending and straightening, and spreading and closing the fingers.
Interphalangeal joints are hinge joints: uniaxial.
They allow only bending and straightening.

items.q: A cricket ball strikes the tip of a straight finger, and the tip now droops. Predict the injury and explain it.
model: The tendon that straightens the fingertip has torn from the distal phalanx.
A small piece of bone may come away with it.
Nothing now pulls the fingertip straight.

check.stem: How many phalanges are in each hand?
check.why: The thumb has two and each finger three: 14 in all.

check.stem: What type of joint is an interphalangeal joint?
Which digit has no middle phalanx?
check.why: The thumb has only proximal and distal phalanges.
